advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an assertion that `_push_lease_cas` reads `_REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS` from the `_ref_lock` module at call time (e.g. monkeypatch `_ref_lock._REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS` and assert the captured `timeout=` kwarg reflects it).
evidence: `push_lease_cas` reads all three at call time: `logger = core.logger` / `core._git(... timeout=core._REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS ...)` (_ref_lock_push.py:115-119)
Module docstring names all three as deliberate/load-bearing: `resolves core._git, core._REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS and core.logger through it at call time` (_ref_lock_push.py:42-44)
test_the_git_patch_point_survives asserts only `calls[0][0][1][0] == 'push'`, never inspecting the `timeout=` kwarg it captures in `**k`
advisory.finding: The call-time resolution of `core._REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS` — one of the three load-bearing attributes the module split explicitly reads through `core` at call time — is never asserted by any test. Only `core._git` and `core.logger` are pinned. A refactor that bound the timeout at import time (against the sibling module rather than the caller) — precisely the failure class the split's docstring warns about — would pass all tests.
scenarios: A future edit binds the remote timeout at import from the sibling module, capturing a stale/default value; the reconciler pushes with the wrong timeout and no test fails.
advisory.suggested_fix: In test_the_git_patch_point_survives_the_module_split (or a new test), monkeypatch `_ref_lock._REMOTE_TIMEOUT_SECS` to a sentinel and assert `calls[0][1]["timeout"] == sentinel` so the third call-time-resolved attribute is pinned like `_git` and `logger`.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Drop `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr` from the resolvability parametrization (or replace it with a behavioral assertion) since it has no production caller, unlike the three push entry points.
evidence: search_files for `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr` in the package returns only the assignment `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr = _push.is_cas_mismatch_stderr` (_ref_lock.py:715) — no caller

The test's own docstring justifies resolvability by citing production callers for `_push_cas`/`_push_delete_cas` (acquire's `_plant`, release's `_delete`, `_cas_advance`'s `_do`) — that justification does not extend to `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr`
The other three parametrized names DO have production callers (`_push_cas` at _ref_lock.py:393,476; `_push_delete_cas` at :422), making their resolvability a genuine NameError-preventing contract
advisory.finding: `test_moved_names_stay_resolvable_at_the_original_module_path` parametrizes over `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr`, but that name (the alias at _ref_lock.py:715) has no production consumer — unlike the other three names, nothing in the package reads `_ref_lock._is_cas_mismatch_stderr`. Asserting its resolvability on `_ref_lock` is a change-detector: a behavior-preserving rename/removal of the alias breaks the test without any observable-behavior change.
scenarios: A later cleanup drops the unused `_is_cas_mismatch_stderr` alias (or renames it); this test fails despite no behavior change.
